Page 3

Warm Up — Bernoulli IVP

Solve the initial value problem:

\[\frac{dG}{dt} + \frac{65}{t}\,G = \frac{4}{t}\,G^2, \quad G(1) = 5.\]

Type: Bernoulli (with \(n = 2\)). Substitute to turn into linear.

Divide through by \(G^2\):

\[G^{-2}\frac{dG}{dt} + \frac{65}{t}\,G^{-1} = \frac{4}{t}.\]

Let \(u = G^{-1}\). Then:

\[\frac{du}{dt} = -G^{-2}\frac{dG}{dt}.\]

Page 4

Substituting and Finding the Integrating Factor

Substituting \(-\dfrac{du}{dt}\) for \(G^{-2}\dfrac{dG}{dt}\) and \(u\) for \(G^{-1}\):

\[-\frac{du}{dt} + \frac{65}{t}\,u = \frac{4}{t}.\]

Multiply through by \(-1\) to get standard linear form (note the negative):

\[\frac{du}{dt} - \frac{65}{t}\,u = -\frac{4}{t}.\]

The integrating factor is:

\[\mu(t) = e^{\int -\frac{65}{t}\,dt} = e^{-65\ln t} = e^{\ln t^{-65}} = t^{-65}.\]

Page 5

Integration and Back Substitution

Multiplying through by \(\mu(t) = t^{-65}\):

\[\frac{d}{dt}\!\left[u \cdot t^{-65}\right] = -\frac{4}{t}\cdot t^{-65} = -4t^{-66}.\]

Integrating both sides:

\[u\,t^{-65} = \int -4t^{-66}\,dt = \frac{-4}{-65}\,t^{-65} + C = \frac{4}{65}\,t^{-65} + C.\]

Solving for \(u\):

\[u = \frac{4}{65} + C\,t^{65}.\]

Back-substituting \(G = \dfrac{1}{u}\):

General Solution:

\[G = \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{\dfrac{4}{65} + C\,t^{65}} = \frac{65}{4 + 65C\,t^{65}}.\]

Page 7

Guided Exercise — Two Mixing Tanks

Suppose you have two tanks, Tank A and Tank B, each containing 100 liters of water.

  1. Tank A: Pure water flows in from an outside source at a rate of 5 L/min.
  2. Inter-tank flow: Liquid is pumped from Tank A to Tank B at 5 L/min.
  3. Recirculation: Liquid is pumped from Tank B back to Tank A at 1 L/min.
  4. Drainage: Tank B drains out to a waste line at 4 L/min.

Let \(a(t)\) be the amount of salt (in grams) in Tank A. Let \(b(t)\) be the amount of salt (in grams) in Tank B.

Find a model for this quantitative situation.

Pictures are useful. Draw a picture.

Page 8

Tank Diagram

Diagram: Two rectangular tanks side by side. Tank A (100 L) is on the left; Tank B (100 L) is on the right. A blue pipe enters Tank A from the left at 6 L/min (pure water inflow). An orange arrow at the top flows from Tank A to Tank B at 6 L/min. An orange arrow at the bottom flows from Tank B back to Tank A at 1 L/min. Tank B has a drain exiting at the lower right at 5 L/min.

We model the amount of salt in each tank using the principle:

\[\text{(change in salt)} = \text{(change in)} - \text{(change out)}.\]

Page 9

Modeling Principle

In general:

\[\binom{\text{change in}}{\text{salt}} = \binom{\text{change}}{\text{in}} - \binom{\text{change}}{\text{out}}.\]

Concentration comes into play. Concentration is the ratio

\[\text{concentration} = \frac{\text{amount of salt}}{\text{amount of liquid}}.\]

The amount of salt flow (in or out) equals concentration times the volumetric flow rate of liquid.

Page 10

Equation for Tank A

For Tank A, the change in salt is determined by what enters and what leaves:

Change in (from Tank B recirculation): concentration \(\dfrac{b}{100}\) times flow rate \(1\) L/min gives \(\dfrac{b}{100} \cdot 1\).

Change out (pumped to Tank B): concentration \(\dfrac{a}{100}\) times flow rate \(6\) L/min gives \(\dfrac{a}{100} \cdot 6\).

\[\frac{da}{dt} = -\frac{6}{100}\,a + \frac{1}{100}\,b.\]

Convention: write \(a\) terms before \(b\) terms.

Page 11

Equation for Tank B

For Tank B:

Change in (from Tank A): \(\dfrac{6\,a(t)}{100}\).

Change out (recirculation back to A plus drainage): \(\dfrac{6\,b(t)}{100}\).

\[\frac{db}{dt} = \frac{6\,a(t)}{100} - \frac{6\,b(t)}{100}.\]

This gives a system of two ODEs:

\[\begin{cases} a' = -\dfrac{6}{100}\,a + \dfrac{1}{100}\,b \\[6pt] b' = \dfrac{6}{100}\,a - \dfrac{6}{100}\,b \end{cases}\]

Page 12

Vector Field Perspective

A useful perspective: think of \(\begin{pmatrix}a'\\b'\end{pmatrix}\) as a vector (arrow) in the plane.

Look at the \(a\)-\(b\) coordinate plane. For any choice of \(a\) and \(b\), the system tells us the vector \((a', b')\) — i.e., how the state \((a,b)\) is changing at that point.

Diagram: A coordinate plane with the horizontal axis labeled \(a\) and the vertical axis labeled \(b\). A point \((a_1, b_1)\) is plotted with a green dot, representing a particular salt-amount state of the two-tank system.

Page 13

Matrix Form and Vector Field

The system can be written in matrix form:

\[\begin{bmatrix}a\\b\end{bmatrix}' = \begin{bmatrix}-\frac{6}{100} & \frac{1}{100}\\[4pt] \frac{6}{100} & -\frac{6}{100}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a\\b\end{bmatrix}.\]

Examples:

At \((a,b) = (1,1)\): plug in to get \(\begin{bmatrix}a'\\b'\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}-5/100\\0\end{bmatrix}\).

At \((a,b) = (1,0)\): plug in to get \(\begin{bmatrix}a'\\b'\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}-6/100\\6/100\end{bmatrix}\).

Observe: Every point in the \(a\)-\(b\) plane gets a vector. This gives a vector field!

Page 14

Vector Field Visualization

The two plots below show the vector field for the system

\[\mathbf{x}' = \begin{bmatrix}x'\\y'\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}f(x,y,t)\\g(x,y,t)\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}-\dfrac{6}{100}\,x + \dfrac{1}{100}\,y\\[6pt]\dfrac{6}{100}\,x - \dfrac{6}{100}\,y\end{bmatrix}.\]
Left plot: A grid of green arrows covering the \(xy\)-plane from \(-4\) to \(4\) on both axes. All arrows point generally inward toward the origin, indicating the system decays to zero. The point \((1,1)\) is marked with a blue dot at \(t = 0\). Right plot: Same vector field, with a red arrow added at \((1,1)\) showing the direction of the solution trajectory starting there. The trajectory spirals inward toward the origin, confirming that both salt amounts approach zero over time.
